title: Gerund and gerundive

objectives.can: Tell the gerund (a verbal noun) from the gerundive (a verbal adjective), and read ad + gerundive as purpose and the gerundive with sum as obligation.

explanation.summary: Latin has two forms in -nd- that English cannot match. The gerund is a verbal noun, the missing cases of the infinitive ('of going', 'for teaching'). The gerundive is a verbal adjective with a passive sense, 'to be taught', that agrees with a noun. Together they give Latin its ordinary ways of saying purpose with *ad* and obligation with *sum*.

sections.heading: Two forms that look alike
body: Both forms are built on the present stem plus *-nd-*: *dandum*, *dandam*, *docendum*, *redeundi*. They differ in what they are.

The gerund is a noun. It is neuter singular, has no nominative (the infinitive does that work) and has no plural. It is found in the genitive (*-ndi*), the dative and ablative (*-ndo*) and the accusative (*-ndum*, only after a preposition). Its sense is active, and it names the action: 'of going', 'by going'.

The gerundive is an adjective of the first and second declensions, *-ndus*, *-nda*, *-ndum*. It has all cases and both numbers, and it agrees in case, number and gender with a noun. Its sense is passive: 'to be given', 'to be strengthened'. The two are told apart by a simple test. If a noun stands beside the form and agrees with it, the form is a gerundive. If it stands alone, with no noun to agree with, it is a gerund.

sections.heading: Ad + gerundive: purpose
body: The commonest use in the Latin Bible is *ad* with an accusative gerundive, to give a purpose. In Acts 5:31, God exalted Christ *ad dandam pœnitentiam Israëli*. The form *dandam* agrees with *pœnitentiam*, accusative feminine singular: literally 'for repentance to be given to Israel', which English says 'to give repentance to Israel'.

Luke 1:79 has *ad dirigendos pedes nostros in viam pacis*. The form *dirigendos* is accusative masculine plural and agrees with *pedes*: 'to direct our feet into the way of peace'. In Romans 15:8, *ad confirmandas promissiones patrum* is the same shape with a feminine plural, 'to confirm the promises of the fathers'.

In these phrases the thing acted on is the noun that the gerundive agrees with, and the sense is passive. English makes the same thing the object of an active verb. Learn to turn one into the other. A careful reader asks first which noun the *-ndus* form agrees with.

sections.heading: The gerund
body: When there is no noun to agree with, the form is a gerund, a noun meaning the action. In 2 Timothy 3:16 scripture is *utilis ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad corripiendum et erudiendum*: 'useful for teaching, for reproving, for correcting and for instructing'. These are neuter accusatives after *ad* and stand without a noun.

The genitive gerund depends on a noun. In Hebrews 4:1, the *pollicitatio* is *introëundi in requiem*: 'the promise of entering into his rest'. In Esther 2:14 the woman has no *potestatem ... redeundi* to the king, no 'power of returning'. The ablative gerund gives the means or the manner. In Acts 10:38 Jesus *pertransiit benefaciendo et sanando*: 'went about doing good and healing'. In Hebrews 8:13 *Dicendo ... novum veteravit prius* means 'in saying new, he made the first old'.

In the Latin of the Church the ablative gerund does more work than in classical prose and often stands where English uses a present participle, 'doing good' or 'saying'. Read it as a way of acting: 'by' or 'in' the doing.

sections.heading: The gerundive with sum: obligation
body: A gerundive with a form of *sum* says what must be done. The gerundive is nominative and agrees with the subject, and the person who must do it is usually in the dative (a dative of agent). In Cassian, *nobis curandus est morbus* means 'the disease must be cured by us': *morbus* is the subject, *curandus* agrees with it, and *nobis* is the agent.

The same shape can mean what is to happen. In Matthew 17:21 Jesus says *Filius hominis tradendus est in manus hominum*: the Son of man is to be handed over. This describes what lies ahead more than a duty, and the sense depends on the verse. This construction is the passive periphrastic conjugation, which the next lesson treats with the others.

sections.heading: What the library can and cannot tell you
body: Many -ndum, -ndo and -ndi forms fit more than one analysis. *docendum* could be a gerund (neuter accusative) or a gerundive (masculine or neuter accusative), and the analyser records the gerundive's label with the gender left open. Only a few words are marked with certainty. The 15 certain gerunds are all from *eo* and its compounds, such as *redeundi*, *introëundi* and *eundum*. The gerundives marked with certainty are those whose gender is plain from the form, such as *dandam* (feminine) or *tradendus* (masculine). The questions in this lesson ask you to apply the test to real verses and do not rely on the automatic label.

misunderstandings: Taking every -ndum form as a gerundive. Without a noun to agree with it, it is a gerund: *ad docendum* has nothing to agree with.
Translating a gerundive with a passive that the English will not bear. *ad dandam pœnitentiam* is 'to give repentance', although Latin says 'for repentance to be given'.
Forgetting the agreement. In *ad dirigendos pedes* the ending of *dirigendos* is plural because *pedes* is plural; a gerund would have the singular neuter ending.
Reading the dative with a gerundive and *sum* as the one who receives. In *nobis curandus est morbus*, *nobis* is the doer: the disease must be cured by us.

deeper.heading: Why Latin prefers the gerundive
body: Classical Latin usually avoids a gerund that takes an accusative object, as in 'for giving repentance' with *dandum* and an accusative. It puts the object in the case of the gerund and turns the gerund into a gerundive that agrees with it. That is why *ad dandam pœnitentiam* is the usual form. Later Latin loosens the rule, and Christian writers use the gerund with an object more freely. Grammarians have debated the history of the forms for a long time, and a reader does not have to settle it.

quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

check.explain: *ad* with a gerundive is a standard way to say purpose. *dirigendos* agrees with *pedes* (accusative masculine plural).

check.prompt: *Filius hominis tradendus est in manus hominum* (words 8–14): what does the gerundive *tradendus* agree with, and what does the phrase say?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.english: And when they abode together in Galilee, Jesus said to them: The Son of man shall be betrayed into the hands of men:
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: Filius; it says that the Son of man is to be handed over
manus; it says 'hands must be given'
check.explain: *tradendus* is nominative masculine singular, agreeing with *Filius*. A gerundive with *est* says what is to be done to the subject: handed over into the hands of men.

check.prompt: *nobis curandus est morbus* (words 13–16): who must do the curing?

quoted.title: Institutes (De institutis coenobiorum)
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: We: nobis is the dative of agent
check.explain: With a gerundive of obligation the doer is in the dative. *morbus* is the subject, and *curandus* agrees with it: the disease must be cured by us.

check.prompt: *relicta pollicitatione introëundi in requiem* (words 4–8): what is *introëundi*, and on what does it depend?

quoted.title: Hebrews
quoted.english: Let us fear therefore lest the promise being left of entering into his rest, any of you should be thought to be wanting.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: A genitive gerundive agreeing with requiem
A perfect participle agreeing with pollicitatione
A genitive gerund depending on pollicitatione: 'the promise of entering'
check.explain: *introëundi* is a genitive form in *-ndi* with no agreeing noun, so it is a gerund: a noun of action. It depends on *pollicitatione*. The phrase *in requiem* is what the entering is into.

check.prompt: *qui pertransiit benefaciendo et sanando omnes oppressos* (words 11–17): what do *benefaciendo* and *sanando* express?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.english: Jesus of Nazareth: how God anointed him with the Holy Ghost, and with power, who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: A purpose: 'in order to do good'
A cause that is still to come
The means or manner of his going about: 'by doing good and healing'
check.explain: Both are ablative gerunds, with *omnes oppressos* as the object of *sanando*. They tell how he went about, and the English present participle 'doing good and healing' is a good rendering.

check.prompt: *nec habebat potestatem ad regem ultra redeundi* (words 22–28): what is *redeundi*?

quoted.title: Esther
quoted.english: And she that went in at evening, came out in the morning, and from thence she was conducted to the second house, that was under the hand of Susagaz the eunuch, who had the charge over the king’s concubines: neither could she return any more to the king, unless the king desired it, and had ordered her by name to come.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: A genitive gerund depending on potestatem: 'power of returning'
check.explain: *redeundi* is a genitive gerund. It depends on *potestatem*: she had no power of returning to the king. It does not agree with any noun.

reading.why: The end of the Benedictus: two phrases of purpose with *ad* and a gerundive, *ad dandam scientiam* and *ad dirigendos pedes*, in four short verses that can be read aloud.
